Q26.text: The academic system encourages absolute sacrifice for the sake of success, which is neither healthy nor fair. The lack of opportunities creates a cutthroat-type of environment, where too often the ones climbing to the top do so at the expense of others, or by forging data to publish in high-impact journals. At the same time, those with families, or other responsibilities - generally women, let's be real -, or those who need to sustain a job to pay for the PhD, cannot afford to sacrifice their entire time to research, and are easily pushed to the sidelines. The latter also speaks to the difficulty for PhDs to compete in a global job market, as the financial burden is widely different around the world. Likewise, PhD programmes vary immensely in quality - a 3-year PhD graduate whose project was spoon-fed to them by their supervisor will not have developed the same skills as a 5-year PhD who had to design their own research project, but they will compete in an almost equal footing for a position.

But regardless I turned out to be a shit scientist -- no publications (inc. in sight), no conferences attended even with a poster, I am not sure whether my research will yield something presentable. I do not know how I will afford rent, savings for the future, taking care of my parents -- I am the only child. I do not know whether I can land an industry job in the competitive environment over-producing PhDs.  I heard about people who get scholarships and earn 30-50% above the typical postdoc salary. They apply for grants and quickly become PIs to earn their lower three figures. Or they aim for green cards through H1B or EB2, paying for the mistake of being born in a shit third-world country, through living off $45k for several years to then end a better paying job in industry. Both options require publishing at least three first author papers, having citations, getting funding, networking -- all the things I don't see myself doing as of now. There are labs that are more collaborative and people end up helping with other peoples' projects and with more papers in the end. I am not in one of them. People who chose different majors -- programming or medicine -- can get bioinformatician or clinical fellow salaries doing same science next to me but earning two times more. Their salaries approaching market because they have a choice. I do not have a choice. Why did no one stop me at any point? How did I end up here? What am I going to do in the future? I think academic system feeds on people like me luring us with promises of meaningful job and hard work paying off and shits us out. It is not healthy to work weekends. It is not healthy to sometimes go months without seeing any progress. It is not healthy to over-sell results in publications just to survive in this environment.

Q26.text: Sadly, the only important criteria for success in academia is the amount of published material. This often leads to rivals among senior and junior researchers, where the former is more likely to get the credit even for work performed by the junior person (e.g. author list on publications). A race for publishing is so intense since most staff contracts (PhD stipends) depend on the amount and impact of publications within a certain time frame (e.g. 3 years for a PhD in life sciences).      Unfortunately, moral standards at some German institutions are at its lowest level: A new research institute that is yet to receive its academic recognition will rather ignore repeated complaints on staff injustice and academic misconduct than risk a bad reputation. Likewise, a young PI will refuse to protect and stand behind a victim of sabotage and pretend all is fine, as long as there is a possibility for a new publication from the person doing the injustice.       PhD students are often subjected to exploitation with no protection since at the end of the day everyone needs that critical reference letter to pursue the next step in an academic career.

Q60.text: Thanks for performing this survey. This is an extremely important topic that is often overlooked. We are looked at as cheap labor (and often young) labor that needs to pay their dues. But often it comes at the cost of our mental and physical health. My mental and physical health has significantly declined over the past 4 years that I've been in my PhD program. I've definitely experienced depression and anxiety, and have had many more visits to the doctor for physical health problems. A back problem from sitting for 12 hours a day at the computer, problems with my hands from typing so much, other problems from increasing my drinking (to cope with stress), a urinary tract infection from holding my urine too long because I don't have time to pee because I am working; I've often put off medical appointments due to lack of time as well. Students often put off their health like they are in survival mode and tell themselves "it's okay to not be healthy for a while" because when you are done with the program you will have time to be healthy. But after years of putting off your health and happiness, living in "survival mode" becomes unbearable. That combined with feeling like you have no control over your own labor nor are getting compensated a livable wage for it can be extremely depressing. Granted some students are predisposed to having more health problems than others as a result of the stressors of a PhD program--however, there are major problems with the system and culture of PhD education that need to be fixed to support student health.

Q26.text: O sistema acadêmico da república tcheca é bastante focado em produção.  Não se importa muito a defesa de uma tese, da ideia em si.  Apenas vejo que o programas de PhD em geral esqueceram da onde vem a sigla Ph.D e não discutem mais as coisas no âmbito argumentativo.  Não importam tanto com o racional do projeto, com a hipótese do projeto... e a defesa argumentativa que deveria ser feita.  Maioria dos projetos vejo que começa simplesmente por que temos dinheiro e estrutura. Mas não porque temos um grande racional e uma justificativa para tentar lançar uma hipótese a ser defendida por provas a posteriori.    Na minha concepção,  Tudo deveria iniciar com uma ideia sólida.  Uma hipótese a qual todos não consigam derrubar com argumentos. Sendo interessante alocar recursos escassos para responder uma pergunta da qual necessita-se de uma resposta a posteriori.    O sistema então acaba valorizando bastante dados soltos, contudo ainda sim são resultados. E acaba desvalorizando o tempo 'perdido' no campo das ideias.   A quantidade muitas vezes parece ser mais importante do que a qualidade . Infelizmente vejo que o sistema recompensa este tipo de mentalidade.  No Brasil (país onde fiz meu mestrado), não era diferente.   Com isso , o sistema que criamos é um sistema preocupado com técnicos. Pessoas que vangloriam por saber determinada técnica.  Pois em teoria, isto traz mais produção.  As pessoas não entendem que aprender técnica é apenas uma questão de tempo e prática. Não precisa de raciocínio lógico. Sendo que em muitos institutos grandes, você de fato tem técnicos e facilities para fazer o trabalho técnico para você.   No entanto, técnica pode ser aplicada mil vezes... mas se não estiver denfendendo uma ideia não fará nenhum sentido fazer por fazer.   Acredito que precisamos fazer um esforço para mudar esta mentalidade nos institutos ao redor do mundo.  A revista Nature é muito conceituada e acredito que ela representa bem a amostragem dos institutos que de fato estão preocupados em mover o mundo através de ideias.    Pedro Zeni

Q26.text: The academic system works on networking and knowing people, including the publication system. Q26.text: Contradictory, honestly. The rhetoric around collaboration and intellectual openness is genuine on the surface, but in practice it runs up against careerism and gatekeeping at every turn. Q16.text: The mandatory coursework has been more of an irritant than I expected -- not because I'm against learning, but because the courses feel disconnected from the problems I'm actually trying to think through. Time ticking boxes is time not spent on research. There's also this creeping anxiety about whether the work translates into something viable, not just academically but in terms of finding a position that values the kind of thinking I want to do.

Q55.text: How political it actually is. Not in some naive 'I didnt know academia was competitive' way -- I knew that. But the degree to which proximity to the right people, the right networks, shapes what gets taken seriously... I genuinely underestimated that. Knowing intellectual work is only part of the equation would've changed how I approached things from day one.

Q41.text: Research-oriented work -- literature synthesis, grant writing, the kind of role where sustained critical thinking is actually the job. Q60.text: Just that I hope the data from this is actually used to improve things, not just filed away. There's a lot of structural dysfunction that gets named in surveys like this and then... nothing changes. I'm cynical about it but I filled this out anyway, so make of that what you will.

Q17.text: The thinking, genuinely. When everything else falls away -- the politics, the box-ticking, the anxiety about what comes next -- there are stretches where you're just deeply inside a problem, and that's hard to replicate anywhere else. Q26.text: Honestly, it's not a meritocracy, and anyone who tells you otherwise has either never looked too hard or has personally benefited from the way things actually work. I've watched genuinely talented people get pushed out while mediocre researchers with the right connections thrive, and thats not a one-off, that's the system functioning as designed. There's real intellectual beauty in the work itself -- I still believe that -- but the institutional layer on top of it is mostly politics dressed up in the language of rigor and excellence.

Q55.text: That your supervisor's political standing in the department matters more than their research quality. I picked mine based on the science, which was pretty naive in hindsight -- turns out who they're on good terms with, who owes them favors, all of that shapes your trajectory more than the actual work does. the science is almost secondary to that stuff.

Q41.text: Community college or four-year college teaching, honestly. I'd love to just be in a classroom, actually engaging with students who want to learn, without all the performance of research output metrics and departmental politics. I'm not gonna pretend I expect a cushy R1 position -- I've seen how that game gets played and I'm not interested in competing for something rigged. Teaching is where I've always gotten the most satisfaction anyway, so might as well lean into it.

Q60.text: Just that I hope whoever is reading these actually does something with them and doesnt just file them away. There's a lot of frustration in academia that gets acknowledged and then quietly ignored, and that pattern is kind of exhausting. The system has real problems -- not just inconveniences, actual structural failures -- and surveys like this only matter if the findings make it somewhere that counts.

Q17.text: The actual research, when I get to just sit with a problem and dig into it without anyone hovering. Biology is genuinely fascinating to me -- there's a reason I came back for a second doctorate -- and those stretches where the work is just the work, no committee meetings or grant theater, those are good. I also really value the students I interact with as a TA. that part reminds me why I got into this in the first place.

Q26.label: Overall, how would you describe the academic system, based on your PhD experience so far?
Q26.text: The academic system encourages absolute sacrifice for the sake of success, which is neither healthy nor fair. The lack of opportunities creates a cutthroat-type of environment, where too often the ones climbing to the top do so at the expense of others, or by forging data to publish in high-impact journals. At the same time, those with families, or other responsibilities - generally women, let's be real -, or those who need to sustain a job to pay for the PhD, cannot afford to sacrifice their entire time to research, and are easily pushed to the sidelines. The latter also speaks to the difficulty for PhDs to compete in a global job market, as the financial burden is widely different around the world. Likewise, PhD programmes vary immensely in quality - a 3-year PhD graduate whose project was spoon-fed to them by their supervisor will not have developed the same skills as a 5-year PhD who had to design their own research project, but they will compete in an almost equal footing for a position.

Q26.text: The academic system is, in many ways, a monument to its own perpetuation -- brilliant at producing scholars who fit its mold, less adept at asking whether the mold actually serves society. Coming in as someone who spent decades outside it, I see both the genuine intellectual richness and structural insularity that limits its reach. honestly, the questions most worth asking are often the ones least rewarded by the system itself.

Q16.text: The thing I didn't fully anticipate is how differently time feels at this stage of life. The academic clock assumes decades ahead -- I'm working with a different calculus, and honestly that sharpens my focus more than it concerns me. the mismatch between institutional timelines and my own is something I navigate constantly.

Q55.text: That the committee relationship matters more than the research plan -- honestly, you can revise a question but you cant easily revise the power dynamics you've locked yourself into. I assumed intellectual alignment would be sufficient; interpersonal fit shapes everything downstream, and that particular lesson arrived later than it should have.

Q41.text: Pro bono research in partnership with NGOs or community organizations -- honestly the credential was never really the point. I came in with a career behind me, and what I want on the other side is the freedom to pursue work that answers to communities rather than grant cycles or tenure committees.

Q60.text: Only that I hope surveys like this one actually inform something -- structural reform, support redesign, something. The data gathering is the easy part; what gets done with it is where good intentions tend to stall. I came to this PhD with enough professional history to recognize the gap between research and institutional change, and I'd be glad if even a fraction of what respondents share here closes it a little.

Q17.text: The permission to pursue a single question deeply, without the fractured attention that professional life demands -- honestly, that's the thing I didn't expect to value as much as I do. There's something almost luxurious about intellectual sustained focus, even when the institutional machinery around it is maddening.

Q26.label: Overall, how would you describe the academic system, based on your PhD experience so far?
Q26.text: As a late career-changer, I have seen the institutional attitude shift from "sink or swim" indifference to a genuine concern with student success. While this is undoubtedly enlightened self-interest on the part of the academy, it is a good first step. The next challenge is preparing grads for real careers. I notice that the concern with the endless postdoc cycle is gaining traction. A societal change, where science is seen not only as credible, but essential to our survival in every sphere, would help create the right atmosphere for bright new minds to flourish and contribute. Here in the USA, this is a problem at present.

Q55.label: With the benefit of hindsight, what one thing do you know now which you wish you'd known about when you started your PhD?
Q55.text: Create a plan early, and refine it as often as necessary. A flawed or incomplete plan is better than no plan at all. Think of your coursework not as an externally-imposed checklist, but as a set of building-blocks for the finished product. Make every course count for something you plan to use. Take the opportunity to tailor electives and directed study coursework to your individual plan.

Q26.text: Honestly, it's a fairly well-disguised pyramid scheme -- the people at the top accrue the most benefit while the idealistic people near the bottom provide inexpensive, motivated labor and absorb most of the instability. The grant funding structure gives PIs every structural incentive to treat students instrumentally rather than as developing scholars, because their career advancement depends on output, not on mentorship. I entered this program believing the system rewarded intellectual curiosity; what I've found is that it rewards grantsmanship and the capacity to extract from those with the least leverage.

Q16.text: The personal dimensions have been harder than I anticipated -- having personal leave denied during a family crisis, and witnessing comments from my PI that made it pretty clear having children would be viewed as a professional liability. These aren't abstract systemic problems; they're specific incidents that have materially shaped how I think about my future in this field.

Q41.text: Teaching at a small liberal arts college, honestly -- somewhere research expectations are minimal and the actual work is instruction. The grant treadmill isn't something I want any part of after this.

Q17.text: The intellectual depth, genuinely -- there's something I still find meaningful in being given time to think carefully about a narrow problem, even when the surrounding structure is hostile to that kind of reflection. My cohort has also been more sustaining than I expected; the peer relationships have compensated, at least partially, for what the supervisory side has failed to provide.

Q26.label: Overall, how would you describe the academic system, based on your PhD experience so far?
Q26.text: It's becoming clear to me that the academic system constitutes a well-veiled pyramid scheme. This is surprising to me, considering success as a scientist requires one to keep up with changing information.  For some reason, there's a blind spot where grad students are concerned.

Q26.label: Overall, how would you describe the academic system, based on your PhD experience so far?
Q26.text: Experience in academia depends greatly on the department, environment, and university one is attending. If one's department is close-knit and very supportive, the experience is great –– some departments are more helpful when it comes to finding funding, helping with housing, etc. It is especially helpful when everyone in your immediate circle acknowledges just how stressful the academic environment can be. I am lucky that I am in an incredibly supportive environment, and I know this reflects on my positive PhD experience. However, that does not discount the struggles that other people may go through, as there are many times where academia can be a very toxic environment –– "publish or perish" is just one contributor to this. Q26.label: Overall, how would you describe the academic system, based on your PhD experience so far?
Q26.text: Slow!!! So many hierarchical layers to go through before being able to make any meaningful change to the system. Having worked both in industry and academia, I also think academia is as money-driven as industry. The only difference being where the money is coming from. But a lot of the time it feels that the research is more tailored to get good publications to get good grants than for science's sake. PhD students (UK) are also kept under a regime that makes them students, hence unable to unionise, while getting many hours out of them for a stipend that is frankly insufficient compared to our level of expertise. Also, the higher up you go, the more male and white-dominated the environment becomes. There's only one full female professor in my whole institute, and I have genuinely never met a black PI or professor since starting my PhD.

Q26.text: Extractive. You come in with some idealism about contributing to science and they grind that out of you pretty fast. the pay keeps you dependent, visa keeps you trapped, and the publication system means your entire worth is tied to outcomes you barely control -- reagents fail, cell lines die, experiments take three years to go nowhere. Supervisor holds all the power with basically zero accountability. I've watched people leave with nothing translatable on their CV, nothing that means anything outside a very narrow slice of academia nobody is hiring in. And for what? The promise of a postdoc in yet another country, away from everyone you love, for maybe a small bump in stipend. It's not a meritocracy, it's a system that runs on people too desperate or too visa-constrained to leave

Q16.text: Grief, honestly. A family member died and I couldn't go home -- visa risk, no money, lab wouldn't approve the time. You just sit with it and keep pipetting. there's no infrastructure for that, no acknowledgment that you're a person whose life exists outside the bench. And the loneliness compounds it. Partner is on another continent, friends have real jobs now. I dont know how people sustain this without something breaking eventually

Q55.text: That the system isn't designed to help you succeed -- it's designed to extract labour from people who are too invested to quit. I wish someone had told me that before I gave up years, a relationship stranded across an ocean, and any shot at normal financial stability for a credential that mostly qualifies you for more of the same.

Q41.text: Industry. Anything that pays real money and doesnt require moving to yet another country for a postdoc that goes nowhere. I have no illusions about staying in academia -- I just need a job that lets me live somewhere my partner can actually join me, and maybe stop worrying about visas for five minutes. not sure what that looks like with a wet lab PhD but I'm looking

Q60.text: Just that I hope someone actually reads these and doesn't file them away as data points. There are real people behind these answers who are exhausted and stuck and watching their lives get smaller every year. The system produces a lot of suffering and calls it training. I dont think more surveys fix that -- but if it helps someone build a case for changing something, then fine. That's why I answered honestly.

Q17.text: Honestly, the science itself, when it actually works. There's maybe an hour every few months where something comes together in the data and you remember why you started. And some of the people -- the other students in similar situations, you build a kind of dark solidarity with them. That's about it though. the rest I'd trade for a salary and a work visa that doesn't expire

Q26.label: Overall, how would you describe the academic system, based on your PhD experience so far?
Q26.text: I studied for over 8 years to be where I am now. I do not have student debt. I was a straight As student in school and in college. But regardless I turned out to be a shit scientist -- no publications (inc. in sight), no conferences attended even with a poster, I am not sure whether my research will yield something presentable. I cannot network or promote myself. I do not write well. If I graduate without a paper, I am looking at a mediocre lab postdoc position at best with median year salary ~$45k. I do not know how I will afford rent, savings for the future, taking care of my parents -- I am the only child. I do not know whether I can land an industry job in the competitive environment over-producing PhDs.  I heard about people who get scholarships and earn 30-50% above the typical postdoc salary. They apply for grants and quickly become PIs to earn their lower three figures. Or they aim for green cards through H1B or EB2, paying for the mistake of being born in a shit third-world country, through living off $45k for several years to then end a better paying job in industry. Both options require publishing at least three first author papers, having citations, getting funding, networking -- all the things I don't see myself doing as of now. There are labs that are more collaborative and people end up helping with other peoples' projects and with more papers in the end. I am not in one of them. People who chose different majors -- programming or medicine -- can get bioinformatician or clinical fellow salaries doing same science next to me but earning two times more. Their salaries approaching market because they have a choice. I do not have a choice. Why did no one stop me at any point? How did I end up here? What am I going to do in the future? I think academic system feeds on people like me luring us with promises of meaningful job and hard work paying off and shits us out. It is not healthy to work weekends. It is not healthy to sometimes go months without seeing any progress. It is not healthy to over-sell results in publications just to survive in this environment.

Two of my close relatives died and I did not come to say my good byes. My boyfriend is doing PhD in a different country. I hate this.

Q26.label: Overall, how would you describe the academic system, based on your PhD experience so far?
Q26.text: In my lab, PhD students are expected to be completely independent with virtually no guidance or mentorship. I feel a worker, not like a student, and for this reason I think it's imperative we form works councils to protect our interests as doctoral candidates from opaque and arbitrary administrative decisions. The academic system appears to prize the publication of high impact papers over more intrinsic values, such as scientific merit, mentoring, and leadership abilities. Although PhD students work extremely hard, we get very little recognition. A high degree of work autonomy and the intellectual challenge of research are the main redeeming qualities, but sometimes fail to compensate for otherwise brutal conditions...

Q26.text: The academic system is honestly pretty complicated — there's a lot of pressure to fit your work into existing frameworks, and that can stifle genuine curiosity sometimes. But I've found real intellectual satisfaction in the process too, so it's not all bad. it feels more like learning to navigate something that wasn't really designed with you in mind, and figuring out how to make it work for you anyway.

Q16.text: Job security after finishing is probably the biggest thing that sits in the back of my mind -- academia doesn't exactly have a lot of stable positions with decent benefits, and I'm pretty clear-eyed about that. it's not paralyzing, but it's always there.

Q55.text: That taking risks — in your research direction, in the questions you ask — is actually worth it even when it doesn't pan out, because that's where the real learning happens. I spent too long in the beginning trying to play it safe and fit into what I thought was expected, and I wish someone had just told me earlier that uncertainty is kind of the point.

Q41.text: A stable research position at a university is the main thing -- ideally somewhere with decent benefits and job security, not necessarily the most prestigious place. I've kind of made peace with the fact that academia has real structural limits, and I'd rather have a sustainable situation than chase the idea of what an academic career is supposed to look like.

Q60.text: Just that I think surveys like this are actually valuable -- it's easy to feel like the structural stuff (job market, funding, the pressure to publish) is just background noise that everyone accepts, but naming it matters. I hope the data's useful to someone trying to make things better, even incrementally.

Q17.text: Honestly, the intellectual freedom is the thing I keep coming back to — like, even within all the constraints, there's still this space to follow a genuinely interesting problem and see where it goes. The moments where something clicks, or a risk you took on a research direction actually pays off, those feel pretty rare and real in a way that's hard to find elsewhere.

Q26.text: There are no incentives for professors to be excellent mentors. This is not because of any individual professor, but is a systemic issue. Government grants are not awarded based on a professor's ability to mentor. Grants are only awarded based on the professor's ability to carry out research. Universities do not hire professors based on their ability to mentor. Universities hire professors based on their likeability, ability to carry out research, ability to acquire research funding, and ability to market their research in the form of publications, talks, and acclaim.

Q60.text: I think the relationship between industry and academia is perverse. Industry profits from public investment in academic research, and has no obligations to provide any societal benefit with those profits. National or non-profit labs should take academic research to the public. Public investment, public profits, societal benefits. The pharmaceutical industry is an exemplar of this relationship. Every drug has relied on public funding, yet no publicly funded patent returns those investments back into scientific grants. This change occurred during Reagan administration when patents became university rather than government grant office property.

Q26.text: Honestly, it's -- at least from where I'm sitting -- a system that was designed for a different era and hasn't really adapted. There's an implicit understanding that PhD students are cheap labor, and because supervisory accountability is basically nonexistent (or very informal), there's no real mechanism to push back when your time gets redirected toward other people's projects rather than your own. I do think the intellectual side can be genuinely stimulating, and I don't want to sound entirely negative because I've learned a lot -- but the structural dysfunction kind of overshadows that. it feels like the system survives on the enthusiasm of people who care too much to leave, which is both its strength and the thing that allows the exploitation to continue.

Q16.text: One thing I haven't mentioned but that does weigh on me is the mental health dimension -- not just my own situation, but the general culture around it. There's an unspoken expectation that you're fine, that you push through, and asking for support feels like admitting incompetence (which is, honestly, worse than admitting weakness in this environment). I've also noticed that the financial side, while technically survivable, leaves almost no margin, which kind of traps you -- you can't easily leave even when the situation becomes untenable. and that absence of a real exit option is its own kind of pressure that I think affects how people behave, including supervisors who know you have limited alternatives.

Q55.text: That the supervisory relationship is essentially unregulated, and that you should treat it more like a professional negotiation than an academic mentorship -- because tbh, no one is going to enforce anything on your behalf if it goes wrong. I think if I'd understood earlier that the power imbalance is structural and not just a personality issue with my specific supervisor, I would have documented everything from day one and pushed much harder to get my own project defined in writing before agreeing to take on other people's work. It sounds cynical but it's really just practical, and I wish someone had said it plainly rather than letting me figure it out the hard way.

Q41.text: Applied bioinformatics in a medical or clinical setting -- something where the work has a clearer real-world impact than academic publishing cycles allow for. I'm not opposed to academia in principle but rn I'd want any academic position to come with a proper institutional setup, not the kind of informal dysfunction I've been navigating. So industry or hospital-adjacent research is probably where I'm headed, honestly.

Q60.text: I hope the data from this kind of survey actually reaches people who have institutional influence, because it's easy for these issues to get acknowledged at the level of "yes, this is a known problem" without anything changing structurally. The supervisory accountability gap in particular feels like something universities could address if they wanted to -- it's not a resource problem, it's a will problem. And I think for people earlier in their PhD who don't yet have the context to recognize exploitation as exploitation, that gap does real damage that's hard to undo later. Anyway, I appreciate the chance to put this somewhere, even if I'm not optimistic it moves the needle much.

Q17.text: The intellectual freedom, honestly -- or at least the version of it that exists when you're actually working on your own problem and not being pulled sideways. There's something genuinely satisfying about going deep into a question that hasn't been answered yet, especially in bioinformatics where the data is always more complicated than you expect and the analysis kind of becomes its own puzzle. I also appreciate the flexibility of the schedule, even if in practice that flexibility gets filled with things I didn't sign up for. and the people -- at the technical level, collaborating with people who care about the same problems is something I don't take for granted, even when the institutional context around it is frustrating.

Q26.label: Overall, how would you describe the academic system, based on your PhD experience so far?
Q26.text: Sadly, the only important criteria for success in academia is the amount of published material. This often leads to rivals among senior and junior researchers, where the former is more likely to get the credit even for work performed by the junior person (e.g. author list on publications). A race for publishing is so intense since most staff contracts (PhD stipends) depend on the amount and impact of publications within a certain time frame (e.g. 3 years for a PhD in life sciences).      Unfortunately, moral standards at some German institutions are at its lowest level: A new research institute that is yet to receive its academic recognition will rather ignore repeated complaints on staff injustice and academic misconduct than risk a bad reputation. Likewise, a young PI will refuse to protect and stand behind a victim of sabotage and pretend all is fine, as long as there is a possibility for a new publication from the person doing the injustice.       PhD students are often subjected to exploitation with no protection since at the end of the day everyone needs that critical reference letter to pursue the next step in an academic career.

Q26.text: The academic system, at least as I've experienced it at ETH, is genuinely meritocratic in many respects -- resources are available, intellectual standards are high, and there's a real culture of collaborative inquiry. I'm aware my vantage point is somewhat privileged, though: strong funding and institutional prestige insulate me from pressures that colleagues elsewhere face more acutely. The main structural gap I'd point to is mentorship quality, which can honestly make or break a PhD regardless of institutional rank.

Q16.text: The main concern that comes to mind is the longer-term competitiveness of the academic job market -- tenure-track positions are genuinely scarce, and even strong institutional training doesn't guarantee a straightforward path. That said, I'm honestly fairly settled about it: my openness to business-technical bridge roles in industry means I dont feel trapped by a single outcome, which makes the uncertainty easier to sit with.

Q55.text: Probably that the quality of day-to-day mentorship matters more than institutional prestige when choosing a supervisor. I chose ETH partly on reputation, which honestly worked out, but I understand now how much variance exists even within top programs -- and how little of that variance is legible before you arrive.

Q41.text: A tenure-track faculty position is my first preference, though I hold that ambition with some pragmatism -- the market is what it is. I'm also genuinely interested in roles that sit at the intersection of technical depth and strategic or organizational problems, the kind of business-technical bridge that a CS background makes accessible. So I'd say academia first, but industry as a meaningful second rather than a fallback I'd be unhappy with.

Q60.text: The experience has been largely positive, and I appreciate the opportunity to reflect on it systematically. If anything, I'd just reiterate that mentorship structures deserve more institutional attention -- it's the one variable that seems most consequential and least visible from the outside.

Q17.text: Honestly, the intellectual community is what I value most -- the density of people working on genuinely hard problems, and the freedom to engage with ideas at depth rather than in service of a quarterly deliverable. There's also something I find pretty sustaining about the autonomy: setting my own research agenda, even within constraints, feels like a meaningful kind of freedom that I dont take for granted.

One thing that does seem to be lacking is a well developed concept of mentoring/career advice. However, given the current demand for Computer Science graduates in industry, career concerns tend to be more about finding an academic or otherwise engaging position, rather than about job security.

Q26.text: Honestly, it feels like a system designed for a very specific type of person -- someone without financial pressures, with family backing, and the luxury of treating a PhD as an intellectual project divorced from economic reality. the accountability structures are weak, especially around supervision, and there's a lot of rhetoric about support that rarely translates into anything concrete when you actually need it.

Q16.text: The financial toll specifically -- I came in carrying undergraduate debt and the stipend doesnt come close to covering what I actually need, so the gap has just widened. And there's something quietly demoralizing about watching that number grow while being told this is an investment in your future, when the future being implied is an academic one I'm not sure I want anymore. I think the mental health piece also gets underplayed institutionally -- there are resources listed on websites but accessing them feels like another bureaucratic task, and by the time you need them you're already too depleted to navigate the process.

Q55.text: That the stipend isn't the full financial picture -- you absorb costs for conferences, software, the kind of professional development thats expected but never funded, and it adds up faster than anyone tells you upfront. I wish I'd done real budget before accepting, rather than assuming the number they quoted was enough to actually live on.

Q41.text: Something outside academia, pretty firmly at this point. the financial reality of postdoc cycles and the uncertainty of tenure-track positions just doesnt work for what I actually need my life to look like -- I have debt, I have family obligations, and I cant keep deferring stability indefinitely. I'm looking at roles in policy, research adjacent sectors, maybe industry research, anything where the work is still meaningful but the compensation reflects that.

Q60.text: The thing I'd want whoever reads this to take away is that the structural problems aren't abstract -- they land on specific people in specific ways, and the people they land on hardest are the ones who came in with the least cushion. First-gen students, students with debt, students whose families depend on them financially. The institutional response to all of this tends to be individual -- see a counsellor, talk to your supervisor, access the support services -- but the problems are systemic and the individual-level responses dont really touch them. I dont think more pamphlets about wellbeing are the answer. what would actually help is stipend transparency, real mentorship accountability, and an honest conversation about the academic job market that doesn't just happen in hushed tones at the end of a conference. I appreciate that this survey exists, I do, but I also hope the data actually goes somewhere.

Q17.text: The intellectual work itself, when I can actually get to it -- there are moments where I'm genuinely absorbed in a problem and it reminds me why I started. that part hasn't gone away. But its harder to access than I expected, because so much of the PhD ends up being about managing everything around the research rather than doing it, and by the time you clear the administrative and financial noise theres less energy left for the thing you actually came here for.

Q26.label: Overall, how would you describe the academic system, based on your PhD experience so far?
Q26.text: Because there are little to no metrics of evaluation for the PhD programme (none for evaluating PhD mentors, advisors etc) there is a lot of variability on how successful each student is and how terribly the PhD process can be. There is a lack of support of the students in many areas.

Q26.text: Brilliant in theory, broken in practice. The incentive structures punish curiosity and reward output metrics -- its turned science into a publishing factory rather than a truth-seeking enterprise.

Q26.label: Overall, how would you describe the academic system, based on your PhD experience so far?
Q26.text: Good things: intellectual freedom. Bad: Glorifying over working, low stipend, competing for grants is stressful, lack of work boundaries on weekends/during holidays, too much emphasis on applied and not basic research. If I could change one thing about academia, it would be to make universities do 70% basic and 30% applied research. The university is starting to look too much like industry- just let grad students do basic research and stop emphasizing man made metrics of success like impact factors and opportunities for application. The best applications often seem to come as by-products of people doing basic research (PCR, CRISPR, etc.). Stop making scientists grovel about their impact, just let them study nature.

Q16.label: Is there anything else not mentioned that has concerned you since you started your PhD?
Q16.text: Peer review needs to be more rigorous; initial screening for falsified data, re-used images, etc. The quality of our peer review determines the quality of our science and collective understanding. We need to revamp this- I am worried about how many poorly designed studies and misinterpretation of results are published, and how it is clouding our body of knowledge and leading us down fields and research paths that just aren't real or true. We need a generation that is more discerning and doesn't just trust something because it is published; in that sense, I'm worried about the state and fate of science.

Q26.text: The academic system seems genuinely invested in producing knowledge but structurally indifferent to the people doing that work. Support structures that would seem obvious -- clear timelines, mentorship infrastructure, some sense of career pathways -- are largely absent or improvised. Honestly, the intellectual community is real and I value it, but the institutional scaffolding around it seems unlikely to sustain most people who enter

Q16.text: The political climate around government hiring has become a real concern -- I'd initially assumed a research-oriented public sector role was a viable endpoint, but budget pressures and ongoing restructuring make that seem increasingly unlikely rn. And being the first student through my program means there's genuinely no one ahead of me to gauge what's actually achievable in the stated timeframe, which makes planning pretty difficult

Q55.text: That the institutional timeline is more aspirational than real — no one tells you that explicitly, and I spent a lot of early energy assuming the program structure was a reliable scaffold rather than a rough sketch. Knowing that sooner would have changed how I paced my first year and how much I relied on formal milestones as meaningful anchors.

Q41.text: Government policy or public sector research is my first preference, though I'm increasingly uncertain about how viable that is given current budget environments. Consulting is a reasonable fallback, and I haven't ruled out academia -- though I'm pretty clear-eyed about what that path actually looks like.

Q17.text: The intellectual community, honestly — conversations with people who are genuinely invested in ideas and willing to engage seriously with your work. That part has exceeded my expectations. The autonomy is also real; for all the structural frustrations, there's something valuable about having sustained time to think carefully about a problem that actually matters to you, even if the conditions around that time aren't always well-designed.

Q26.label: Overall, how would you describe the academic system, based on your PhD experience so far?
Q26.text: There isn't a lot of sympathy for students going through the process. Advisers and mentors have the mindset of "well I did it, so you should be able to do it too" in regards to work-life balance, low income, and general stress levels. They don't consider what going through the system has done to them or whether it impacted them negatively. In addition, many advisers have chosen to enter academia; therefore, their career advice is generally targeted to that area.

Q26.text: Broken, honestly. The incentive structure rewards prestige accumulation over actual mentorship or pedagogical quality, which means the people running labs are often the worst-equipped to run them -- mine included. My PI is technically brilliant and almost completely absent as a mentor, and the system doesn't just allow that, it selects FOR it. Funding flows to grant-generators, not to good advisors. I do think reform is possible, but it would require rethinking how faculty are evaluated at a structural level, and the people with power to change that have no incentive to. So here we are.

Q16.text: The financial piece, tbh. Stipends haven't kept pace with cost of living in any serious way, and the implicit ask is that you accept near-poverty wages because you're "investing in your future." But that calculus breaks down completely when you're staring down student debt and trying to figure out if you can afford to start a family before you're 35. And the people who designed this system didn't have to make that trade-off -- so they don't see it as a problem.

Q55.text: That advisor fit is EVERYTHING, and the institution will not protect you if you pick wrong. I wish someone had told me to treat the advisor selection process like a job interview — not just "is this person doing cool science" but "will this person actually invest in my development." I did the former and completely skipped the latter, and I've been paying for it ever since. Talk to current and former students, ask direct questions about communication style and career support, and if a PI can't name a single student they've helped transition into a non-academic role, walk away. The science can be great and the mentorship can still be a disaster -- those things are entirely independent, and nobody tells you that at the start.

Q41.text: Management consulting, executive recruiting, or policy work — something that uses analytical skills without the dysfunction of academic career tracks. I'm done with the idea that the only legitimate outcome of a PhD is a postdoc and then a faculty position that may or may not exist. The financial reality of staying in academia doesn't work for me rn, and honestly neither does the culture.

Q60.text: Just -- thank you for doing this research. These issues don't get taken seriously at the institutional level because the people who could act on them have already made it through the system and rationalized the suffering as character-building. The stipend problem is real, the mentorship accountability gap is real, and the implicit promise that "it'll all be worth it" is increasingly a lie for anyone who isn't already independently wealthy or willing to defer every major life decision indefinitely. If any of this data actually reaches policymakers or university leadership, I hope it's presented without the usual softening. The PhD experience for a lot of people is genuinely not okay, and treating it like a series of minor friction points misses the structural rot underneath.

Q17.text: Honestly, the intellectual environment is genuinely something I'd miss. Being surrounded by people who care deeply about hard problems, having access to seminars and conversations that don't exist outside academia -- that part is real, and I don't want to pretend otherwise. I also still love the actual science, the genomics questions I'm working on are legitimately interesting and I doubt I'll get to engage with them at this level anywhere else. But I'd be lying if I said the enjoyment hasn't been steadily hollowed out by everything surrounding the work itself. The thing I enjoy most has basically become the thing I'm grieving as I prepare to leave it.

Q26.label: Overall, how would you describe the academic system, based on your PhD experience so far?
Q26.text: Broken. The wages are skewed. The incentives for faculty to publish in high impact factor journals make graduate students not have as many publications. There's fierce competition for grants which incentivizes cheating. The goal for the graduate student is to graduate and find employment but the goal for the faculty is to produce research and papers, thus these are at conflict. As a grad student becomes well trained, the faculty don't want to let them graduate because they have cheap, well trained, labor. Academic postdoc positions are the same. They're lowly paid but highly competent individuals. Faculty in universities still aren't aware of the data regarding competition for new faculty positions (despite serving on search panels). The whole system is broken.

Q16.label: Is there anything else not mentioned that has concerned you since you started your PhD?
Q16.text: The biggest, most overwhelming concern for the entirety of my PhD is trying to find good employment afterwards that can cover my student debt and allow me to start a family. Unfortunately, academic postdoc positions in the US do not pay enough to do this, which means I have to find a non-default path.

Q55.label: With the benefit of hindsight, what one thing do you know now which you wish you'd known about when you started your PhD?
Q55.text: Good science and good management/leadership do not overlap. My PI is a great scientist but he is a TERRIBLE manager. This is likely why the average time to degree for my lab is 8 years when the department average is 6.5. He's incredibly hands off, provides no positive feedback, and discourages many things. You have to fight tooth and nail to get what you want unless you're his favorite student.

Q41.label: What type of career are you interested in pursuing after your graduate degree?
Q41.text: One that intersects with the life sciences but doesn't require bench research. I'd be happy continuing computational (genomic) research. I enjoy meetings and administrative/leadership/management work. Perhaps a policy analyst and strategy position. I'm currently targeting management consulting, executive recruiting, and policy analyst positions for application.

Q60.label: Thank you for taking part in the survey. Are there any more comments you would like to make?
Q60.text: We don't have an excess of people with PhD degrees. The world needs more highly educated people. We have a broken system that provides incentive for poor quality of life for graduate students and postdocs -- low pay, aggressive competition, long hours, discouragement from leaving the academic environment. This can be fixed, but it needs to be a top-down move away from the publish or perish environment. Even more faculty positions aren't necessary. Staff research positions would be great. Tenure-track teaching positions (divide the labor so some faculty are almost full time research, many are teaching) would make a significant difference. Put hard caps on graduate programs (6 years) to force program progression. Many people in my program don't defend their prospectus until year 5 which is COMPLETELY inappropriate. There is no department or university recourse for this.

Q16.text: My own skill gaps, honestly. Q55.text: That you can't just absorb technical skills passively by being around people who have them. Q26.text: Honestly? Broken. It's a system designed to extract as much labor as possible from people who are too passionate or too trapped to leave. The pay is insulting, the timelines are unpredictable, and there's this unspoken expectation that you should be grateful for the privilege of suffering through it. Q16.text: Mental health is the big one. I've watched multiple labmates go on leave for anxiety or depression, and I've had my own stretches that were honestly scary. nobody talks about it openly -- there's still this stigma about struggling emotionally in academia. And the isolation of being stuck in one city for years, watching friends from undergrad move freely and build actual lives, that weighs on you in ways I didnt anticipate

Q55.text: That the academic job market was basically already dead before I even started. I spent years thinking if I worked hard enough and published enough it would work out -- nobody told me the math just doesnt add up anymore, that there are hundreds of PhDs competing for every tenure-track opening. I wish someone had been brutally honest about that instead of letting me figure it out in year four.

Q41.text: Industry -- staff scientist or a research role in government/national labs. Honestly I'm done with academia. No postdoc, absolutely no interest in the PI track. I just want to do actual science without having to beg for grants or manage a lab full of grad students I cant pay properly.

Q26.text: I think that it's archaic and it presupposes that you're going into academia, which is not true anymore. A Ph.D. should take no more than 4 years like it does in Europe. I don't know why we spend so much time being miserable in American academia, especially since statistically, most of us won't end up as principal investigators anyway. Shorten the programs and get us out so we can actually enjoy our lives.

Q55.text: That I'd be this miserable for most of it. Sure, I'm likely to increase my job prospects and lifetime earnings, but at what cost? I've given almost 6 years of my life to being stuck at this, not being paid what I'm worth and being forced to stay in an area of the country I no longer want to live in. Q55.label: With the benefit of hindsight, what one thing do you know now which you wish you'd known about when you started your PhD?
Q55.text: There are far more opportunities available for postgraduate students in the USA/EU, many of my friends and colleagues in the field who did their Masters degree abroad easily found PhD positions at top ranking institutions despite having no publications in the field (or often any publications at all) and mediocre grades. As a department we also regularly experience what we perceive as discrimination from reviewers towards third world universities, even when the results are objectively valuable and can be quickly reproduced with no effort (such as running a script with fully free and open source code). Many reviewers force us to cite their own papers in the manuscript before accepting our publication (despite being anonymous it is obvious when the authorship fields of these papers all contain the same researcher). Often the work is not significant or the results are less competative than other papers already cited in the manuscript.  In short it is very difficult (but certainly possible) to get in to the right networks for your career if you're coming from the wrong institution. The quality of your research is largely irrelevant, even in fields where problems have objective and established metrics for the quality of solutions.

Q26.text: Structurally broken in a way thats kind of hard to overstate. The system runs on the assumption that passion for research justifies poor pay and exploitative conditions -- which is honestly just a mechanism for extracting cheap labor from people who care too much to walk away. I went through PI change and had to restart two years in, and throughout all of that the pay was below what any comparable qualified position would offer. There's real intellectual value in the work, I genuinely believe that, but the system has figured out how to weaponize that belief against the people doing the work.

Q16.text: The job market is a constant background anxiety that nobody really wants to talk about openly — academia produces far more PhDs than it has permanent positions for, and everyone knows it but the system keeps running as if that isnt true. So there's this weird cognitive dissonance where you're being trained for a career that statistically won't be available to you. I've made peace with the fact that I'm probably not going for a tenure track position, which is partly why science communication appeals to me, but it took a while to stop feeling like that was admitting defeat. And honestly the mental health side of things is underacknowledged -- the isolation, the imposter syndrome, the way your whole identity gets tied to whether your experiments work or your supervisor is having a good week. Those arent small things.

Q41.text: Science communication, primarily — I want to stay connected to research but move into a role where the output actually reaches people outside of academia. I'm also open to research-adjacent roles in science policy or at research institutions that arent strictly academic. A tenure track position isn't really on my radar anymore, and I'm honestly at peace with that.

Q17.text: The intellectual freedom, honestly -- being able to spend my days actually thinking about hard problems rather than executing someone else's tasks feels like a genuine privilege, even when everything else is frustrating. I also really value the people you meet in research; there's a particular kind of conversation you can only have with someone who's also three years deep into something obscure and genuinely cares about it. those connections have been one of the better parts of this, even when the structural conditions are bad.

Q26.text: The academic system right now is outdated and based on the notion we should work because we are lucky to be doing our hobbies. my PhD should not be seen as an hobby but as a normal job and entitled to the same benefits/rules as a normal job

Q16.label: Is there anything else not mentioned that has concerned you since you started your PhD?
Q16.text: The lack of respect for my job as a PhD student from the academy, some of my peers and society in general. My PhD is a job, I work full time on it and however I am only payed 50% (in Germany) of my salary because I am "student". When I complain that this is unfair, that I am not being payed for my full work hours or my extra hours (that are always expected of me as a PhD student); I am told that 1) I should be grateful for even getting paid, other disciplines are not 2) I benefit from student discounts so I should not complain for receiving less (I would happily give away my student discounts if I was payed a full salary!) 3) I should be happy because I am doing my passion job (passion is not going to feed me in my retirement). Not being entitle to a full salary, extra hours or even a contract that will allow us to receive some help after our working years is destroying our future before it even starts.

Q55.label: With the benefit of hindsight, what one thing do you know now which you wish you'd known about when you started your PhD?
Q55.text: I did not start my PhD directly after the masters, I was working sometime as a research assistant. So by the time I decided to do a PhD I knew exactly why I was doing it and what were some of the possible challenges. As such I was prepared to keep going despite having to change my first PI (due to PI sickness) and restarting my PhD after 2 years and despite having a new PI now that is not meeting my expectations. So, I do think i was prepared to do a PhD when I started. Personally, from what I see around me, I would just tell everyone to not do a PhD right after the master/bachelor but to take their time and to find if a PhD is really what they want to do.

Q26.text: Universities need better financing. There are not enough opportunities to get employed after the PhD. There is a huge uncertainty. I am lucky enough to have a great supervisor with reasonable demands, who even gives me freedom in research and supports my creativity. I believe that it is not about the system, but the individuals in it. I think our academic system has approved in the recent years and that PhD student get more support, but most of the problems can't be easily solved by other system changes. As long as PhD students are viewed by most as a cheap workforce to exploit, instead of young scientists with bright ideas and hopeful future, the academia can't move much further.

Q26.text: The academic system, at least as I've experienced it, functions less like a coherent institution and more like a collection of competing fiefdoms where resources are scarce and transparency is largely absent -- and that structural dysfunction affects everything from lab access to funding allocation, which makes it extraordinarily difficult for students who don't already have strong internal alliances to navigate effectively. Honestly, there's genuine intellectual richness here, and I don't want to dismiss that, but the bureaucratic and political dimensions are an exhausting overlay that no one warns you about going in. I came in with clear research goals and a realistic sense of the challenges, but I wasn't prepared for the degree to which institutional inertia and faculty politics could simply block progress that had nothing to do with the quality of the work itself.

Q16.text: The personal cost of the institutional dysfunction I've already described -- in terms of time lost, stress accumulated, and genuine uncertainty about whether my research trajectory will ever stabilize -- is something I find difficult to fully articulate, because it bleeds into everything from sleep to relationships to the basic question of whether continuing is rational given the opportunity costs involved for someone at my career stage. I also think the isolation of being a mature-age student is pretty consistently underestimated; the informal support networks that seem to sustain younger students don't map well onto my situation, and administrative failures carry different weight when you're making decisions that affect life already substantially built rather than one just starting out.

Q55.text: That the political landscape of the department -- who controls lab space, who has faculty alliances, which supervisors are actually funded versus aspirationally funded -- matters as much as, if not more than, the intellectual fit of the research itself, and that going in without that map means you can spend the first year or more just trying to understand a geography that insiders treat as obvious common knowledge. honestly, nobody tells you this.

Q41.text: Neuroscience research, ideally in a role that lets me integrate my background across microbiology, statistics, and psychology -- I came into this specifically to build something with that breadth, and that hasn't changed despite everything, though I'm increasingly realistic about the structural barriers that make academic positions difficult to secure without the kind of institutional support I've found pretty inconsistent so far.

Q60.text: I'd just add that I hope this research reaches people who actually design and administer doctoral programs, because the gap between what institutions say they offer and what students encounter -- particularly those arriving with substantial professional histories and different expectations -- is significant and, I think, largely invisible to faculty and administrators who shape the experience from positions of relative insulation. The funding shortfalls and access problems I've described aren't unique to my situation, and honestly that's probably the most concerning part of it.

Q17.text: The intellectual depth of the work itself -- actually sitting with complex problems that span disciplines and slowly building something that didn't exist before -- is genuinely satisfying in a way I didn't fully anticipate, and honestly it's what keeps me here despite everything else. The research vision hasn't dimmed, even when the institutional context around it has been kind of relentlessly frustrating.

Q26.label: Overall, how would you describe the academic system, based on your PhD experience so far?

The benefit is I am not tied to any one lab but it increases the stress around the experimental stages of my degree due to not gaining access to a lab or failing to get funding. I was very disappointed by the faculty allowing students to be enrolled part time but work full time as this also was not reflected in lab availability as well as very costly in lab equipment and consumables being used at a full time rate rather than a part time rate which drained the lab budget causing the lab to almost run out of money and engage in talks of letting go of the post docs because of funding issues around ability to pay them.

Q26.text: The academic system has significant structural flaws that are rarely addressed at institutional level. Supervision quality varies enormously, yet there are few mechanisms to hold supervisors accountable when they're unavailable or disengaged -- and students bear the consequences in delayed graduations and stalled publications. There's also a disconnect between the intellectual rigour the system demands and the practical support it provides, which I think drives a lot of unnecessary attrition.

Q16.text: The mental health dimension is something I think gets systematically underacknowledged. There's an expectation of resilience that functions more like justification for inadequate support structures than a genuine institutional value. I've also found the precarity of academic career pathways more concerning than I anticipated -- not just personally, but as a broader structural issue affecting whether the best researchers actually stay in the field long-term.

Q55.text: The importance of supervisor accountability structures — or rather, their absence. I assumed institutional frameworks would ensure adequate oversight, but in practice there's very little recourse when a supervisor's clinical commitments consistently crowd out their mentorship responsibilities. Knowing that upfront, I'd have negotiated more explicit expectations around availability and publication timelines before accepting the position.

Q41.text: Independent research, ideally in a setting that isn't wholly dependent on grant cycles -- though I'm also genuinely drawn to science writing or editorial roles. The publication barriers I've encountered have made me think more carefully about how research gets communicated, and that's kinda shaped my thinking about where I could have the most impact outside of a traditional academic track.

Q17.text: The intellectual freedom to pursue questions that feel genuinely consequential. Despite the structural frustrations, there's something that's hard to replicate about being embedded in a research environment where the problems are real and unsolved. I also value the collegial dimension -- conversations with peers who are equally invested in making sense of complex systems, even when institutional support is thin. Honestly, those interactions have probably sustained me more than any formal mentorship structure has.

Q26.label: Overall, how would you describe the academic system, based on your PhD experience so far?
Q26.text: There is a lack of standardization when it comes to how faculty members supervise their trainees, which leads to the students' experience being heavily dependent on the supervisor's personality and management style. Supervision duties should be fully enforced to ensure that professors fulfill their supervisory responsibilities.

Q60.text: I would like to add a common issue that graduate students in biomedical research within my department face whenever they are supervised by medical doctors, which is lack of accessibility. Due to the demanding schedule medical doctors usually have, it is not easy for them to balance between their clinical and research duties. Personally, I found that the clinical and administrative responsibilities are almost always prioritized over supervisory duties. Sometimes, two months or more pass before I have face-time with my supervisor, and I end up seeking help from other principal investigators. I wish the department was more flexible regarding appointing co-advisors in case the principal advisor fails to demonstrate commitment to mentoring their trainees.

Q26.text: Honestly, it's exploitative in ways that have been so thoroughly normalized that pointing it out feels almost naive. Your labor — your ideas, your hours, your intellectual energy — flows upward to support your advisor's reputation and grant portfolio, and the PhD credential is dangled as sufficient justification for all of it. The intellectual content of the work is genuinely interesting to me, and that's the only part I'd defend with any conviction. But the institutional structure around it is absolutely ruthless in how it captures people who are too far in to walk away

Q16.text: The mental health dimension is something I genuinely wasn't prepared for. There's a kind of low-grade, persistent dread that builds when your professional identity and your sense of self-worth are both tied to a single relationship with someone who has near-total power over your timeline -- and I've watched colleagues deteriorate and convince themselves it's normal. The career pipeline mythology also concerns me, honestly: this quiet institutional consensus that industry or teaching represents failure, when those paths are more sustainable and better compensated. I came in believing the prestige narrative. I dont anymore.

Q55.text: That the advisor relationship is the whole ballgame, not one factor among many. I spent too long thinking good work would speak for itself, and it doesnt -- your progress, your timeline, your mental state, all of it is downstream of whether that one person is functional and actually invested in your success rather than just your output.

Q41.text: Industry or applied work — data science, consulting, maybe high school teaching if I want something more humane. The prestige track honestly stopped appealing to me a while ago, and I'm not gonna pretend otherwise. Better pay, better hours, and you're not dependent on one person's mood for your entire career trajectory.

Q60.text: The structural incentives reward exactly the wrong things, and the people who end up thriving are often the ones best at managing optics rather than doing genuinely rigorous work. I've made peace with that to some degree — it just means the credential is the goal, not the culture. I hope this feedback is useful to someone, though I'm honestly not optimistic that survey data moves the needle on any of this.

Q17.text: The intellectual substance of the work itself, honestly — that's the only part that's held up. There's something genuinely satisfying about engaging with hard problems, and when the research is actually moving it can feel like the only thing making the rest of it worth tolerating. I dont want to oversell it, but that part is real.

Q26.label: Overall, how would you describe the academic system, based on your PhD experience so far?
Q26.text: I have a very dismal view of the academic system in general. The majority of my work has almost nothing to do with "education" and instead is truly work being done for my professor that has very little chance of benefiting me or advancing my career independently. In the resource constrained environment of University research, I understand the structural advantage of using a large army of underpaid/overworked graduate students to slog through the work, but the system seems to avoid any sense of good management or efficient work/support. The majority of my time is wasted, but because my time is so inexpensive, this is viewed as acceptable.

Q26.text: The academic system, at least in my experience, operates on surplus labor extraction dressed up as passion and vocation. Attitude from faculty and PIs that your time is fundamentally theirs, attitude from institutions that mental health deterioration is a personal failing rather than a structural outcome, attitude from the broader culture that suffering is a rite of passage rather than policy failure — all of it compounds into something genuinely harmful. I've watched colleagues leave mid-program, I've watched myself develop anxiety and physical symptoms I didn't have four years ago, and I still can't point to single structural mechanism that would prevent the next cohort from going through the same thing. It needs fundamental reform, not wellness workshops and mindfulness seminars tacked onto an unchanged labor model.

Q16.text: The financial precarity is something I didn't fully anticipate — stipends that haven't kept pace with cost of living, the expectation that you'll supplement your income through teaching or casual work on top of a full research load, the way funding insecurity gets used as a kind of behavioral lever to keep students compliant. I've also been genuinely surprised by how isolated the experience can be, even within a nominally collaborative department, and how little of that social isolation gets named or addressed. And honestly, the job market situation has started to feel like the cruelest part — four or more years of labor, health costs, and opportunity cost, feeding into a market where the odds are objectively not favorable. I'm leaving for industry partly because of that calculus, and I don't think I'm an outlier.

Q55.text: That the problems aren't personal failings — they're structural, and the culture is actively invested in making you believe they are. I spent probably two years trying to self-optimize my way out of situations that weren't mine to fix, which honestly cost me a lot in terms of health and time. if I'd understood that earlier, I would have set harder limits sooner and made the decision to leave on my own terms rather than reaching this level of exhaustion first.

Q41.text: Pharmaceutical industry — specifically clinical outcomes research or health economics. I've been moving toward that decision for a while now, and at this point it feels less like a choice and more like the only option that doesn't require me to keep absorbing the costs this system asks of you indefinitely.

Q60.text: Just that I hope data from surveys like this actually reaches people with the power to change institutional policy, rather than being filed away and cited in a report that nobody acts on. The experience has been genuinely damaging in ways I didn't anticipate, and I think the sector owes future students something better than what currently exists. I'm leaving academia, and honestly I think that says everything.

Q17.text: Honestly, the intellectual work itself — when I can actually access it without the administrative and interpersonal noise getting in the way. There are moments, fewer now than at the start, where the research genuinely absorbs me and feels worth doing. I also valued the autonomy early on, the sense that I was directing something. But it's hard to answer this question cleanly at this stage because most of what I used to enjoy has been worn down by everything else, and I'm not sure how much of my current feeling reflects the work itself versus just exhaustion with the surrounding conditions.

Q26.label: Overall, how would you describe the academic system, based on your PhD experience so far?
Q26.text: Needs major reform. There should be standards for living and mental health that all programs across fields should be required to abide by. There should also be annual training for faculty (regardless of tenure/career level) on how to mentor students.

Attitude from faculty/PIs that you should be grateful for opportunities even if they cost you significantly more time than what you are paid. Attitude from faculty/PIs that you should always be willing to take on more work for a publication. Expectations from faculty/PIs that you work until the job is done even if it requires you to put in 50% to 100% more time than what you are supposed to work and what you are paid for. Putting off having children because I need to finish my PhD and get a job that pays a decent wage. Always feeling like you have to much work that you can never relax.

Q60.label: Thank you for taking part in the survey. Are there any more comments you would like to make?
Q60.text: Thanks for performing this survey. This is an extremely important topic that is often overlooked. We are looked at as cheap labor (and often young) labor that needs to pay their dues. But often it comes at the cost of our mental and physical health. My mental and physical health has significantly declined over the past 4 years that I've been in my PhD program. I've definitely experienced depression and anxiety, and have had many more visits to the doctor for physical health problems. A back problem from sitting for 12 hours a day at the computer, problems with my hands from typing so much, other problems from increasing my drinking (to cope with stress), a urinary tract infection from holding my urine too long because I don't have time to pee because I am working; I've often put off medical appointments due to lack of time as well. Students often put off their health like they are in survival mode and tell themselves "it's okay to not be healthy for a while" because when you are done with the program you will have time to be healthy. But after years of putting off your health and happiness, living in "survival mode" becomes unbearable. That combined with feeling like you have no control over your own labor nor are getting compensated a livable wage for it can be extremely depressing. Granted some students are predisposed to having more health problems than others as a result of the stressors of a PhD program--however, there are major problems with the system and culture of PhD education that need to be fixed to support student health.

Q26.text: It's genuinely pretty good at training you to think rigorously, and I value that more than I expected to. But the system is also weirdly indifferent to whether you're actually okay -- like, the institution cares about your output, not you as a person. Q55.text: That the institution isn't actually looking out for you in any holistic sense -- it tracks your progress, sure, but nobody really checks whether you're okay as a person. I wish I'd built my own support structures earlier instead of assuming department would catch me if things got bad.

Q41.text: Honestly I'm still figuring it out, which is a little uncomfortable to admit at this stage. Science communication keeps pulling at me -- there's something appealing about actually bridging that gap between research and the public that I feel like academia just ignores.
