Q60.text: Just that I hope this kind of research actually gets used to improve things -- not just filed away. Q26.text: Honestly, it's more competitive and isolating than I expected. Everyone is so focused on their own output that there's very little sense of shared purpose or community. I came in hoping to collaborate, and instead found a lot of closed doors and absent supervisors. it feels like the system rewards individual achievement at the expense of everything else.

Q16.text: The mental health side of it, honestly. I didn't expect to feel this lonely in an environment full of smart people. there's no real support structure, and it took me a while to realise that was by design, not accident. That's probably the thing that concerns me most.

Q55.text: That the culture of academia is baked in early -- you can't really change it from inside a PhD. I wish someone had told me that the isolation I was feeling wasn't a personal failure, it's just how the system is built. Knowing that sooner would have saved me a lot of energy trying to fix something that wasn't mine to fix.

Q41.text: Teaching, definitely -- maybe some outreach work too. I'm not super interested in a traditional research career after this experience, tbh. I'd rather be somewhere that actually values connection and community.

Q60.text: Just that I hope this research actually leads somewhere. Surveys like this feel important, but it's hard not to wonder if the findings just sit in a report somewhere. The problems I've described -- the isolation, the absent supervisors, the culture of individualism -- they're not new. People have been saying this for years. I guess I'm a bit cynical about whether anything changes, but I filled this out because some part of me still hopes it might.

Q17.text: Honestly, the work itself -- when I'm actually deep in a problem and it clicks, that part is still good. I do genuinely care about the research questions I'm exploring. And there are occasional conversations with other students where you remember why you came here. But those moments feel rarer than they should, kind of isolated highlights in an otherwise pretty draining experience.

Q26.label: Overall, how would you describe the academic system, based on your PhD experience so far?
Q26.text: I can repeat what I wrote above. I think there is too much time alone. I had expected to become part of a creative and established research group, but there is basicaly no group. Everyone is occupied with their own businesses. There is also no proper introduction for phd-students at the department and you are left alone to figure out where to go and what to do. And that you are trained to think egoistic and not collaborative is not constructive! At least not to me.

Q16.label: Is there anything else not mentioned that has concerned you since you started your PhD?
Q16.text: The unhealthy egoistic culture in academia. I think high-quality research evolves from smart people working together thinking out solutions together, however, the competitiveness between researchers and the little available funding destroy this possibility. I think it is an unhealthy culture to be part of. Furthermore, publications in high-impact journals are valued more than for instance teaching experience and ability when you apply for permanent positions. I think society looses a lot on this, as we end up with a lot of (again) egoistic people at the universities, who then is forced to teach, but feel that it is a waste of time and the result is low-quality teaching.

Q55.label: With the benefit of hindsight, what one thing do you know now which you wish you'd known about when you started your PhD?
Q55.text: That my main-advisor is not a group person but works better individually, which is completely opposite of me. That both my main supervisors always travel and very seldom are present at the department (contributing to even less research group feeling).

Q26.text: The academic system is intellectually rich but deeply hierarchical. the power balance between supervisor and student can be quite limiting -- we lose a lot of autonomy that could otherwise fuel genuine curiosity. I find myself wondering what could have been different if I had understood the system better from the start.

Q16.text: One thing that has stayed with me is the realization -- quite late -- that we had the kind of research background institutions like Yale or MIT actively look for. no one tells you this at the start, and by the time you understand how the system works, certain doors have already closed. That quiet missed opportunity has honestly been hard to sit with.

Q55.text: That we had translational research profile that top institutions genuinely value. I wish someone had told us this early -- not after we were already committed to a path where pivoting became so much harder. The academic hierarchy doesn't really prepare you to see your own market value, and that gap cost us real options.

Q41.text: Research in industry -- I find the idea of science with real-world application genuinely compelling, and honestly the academic structure has made me less interested in staying within it long-term. A research role in industry feels like a place where we can do meaningful work without the same power dynamics shaping everything.

Q60.text: Just that we hope this kind of research actually leads somewhere -- that the data collected here helps make the PhD experience less opaque for future students. The system doesnt have to work the way it does, and honestly the fact that so few people talk openly about the power dynamics or how to navigate institutional opportunities is part of what makes it so hard. We figured things out too late. Maybe others won't have to.

Q17.text: Honestly, the intellectual side of it -- the actual science, the questions we get to sit with and try to answer. There's something genuinely exciting about being at the edge of what's known, and that hasn't gone away despite everything else. I guess that curiosity is what keeps us going even when the structural side of things feels pretty draining.

Q26.label: Overall, how would you describe the academic system, based on your PhD experience so far?
Q26.text: Research opportunities are great but we cannot do what we want. It is a job where you work for a boss (supervisor) and try to learn as much as possible both from the research as well as other experiences. Even though one is interested in science but the constant pressure does not help to fuel it but kills the motivation.

Q16.label: Is there anything else not mentioned that has concerned you since you started your PhD?
Q16.text: The concern is the bubble we live in and created by the people around us. We do what our supervisor asks us to do and tries to manipulate or motivate (difficult to differentiate) to do more and more. But what is enough??

Q55.text: The research possibilities at other universities. Being from a specific background, we do not know that we can apply for other programs as well since the research is very translational nowadays. If I had known, I would have applied to labs in Yale, Harvard, and MIT.

Q26.text: Based on my experiences there are major flaws with the academic system, however this does appear to be is is centralised within my institution. I have seen this have a huge negative impact on peoples research and limited the opportunities for students to gain experience in other areas and techniques out-with the main topic. However, I have seen the system in other countries during research visits, where other institution drive forward the idea of collaboration and actively encourage this, something I feel all should be included in all PhD programmes.

Q26.text: Honestly? Bloated and inefficient. The system rewards people who are good at writing grants and playing politics, not people who are actually good at doing research. And the curriculum -- god, so much of it is just busywork with no real connection to what you'd do in industry or even a government lab. I've spent years on learning stuff that'll be useless the second I leave. There's also this weird cult of suffering, like the more miserable your PhD is, the more legit it somehow is. It's a broken machine and everyone knows it but nobody wants to say it out loud.

Q16.text: The opportunity cost thing keeps me up at night, honestly. Every year I'm here is another year my peers in industry are building actual products, getting promotions, compounding experience. I'm gonna come out the other side with a fancy title and a CV full of papers nobody reads, competing against people who've been doing real work this whole time. And the mental health stuff -- I didn't expect how isolating it would be. You're just grinding away on this hyper-niche problem and there's no feedback loop, no sense of progress, just vibes and your supervisor's mood that week. That's been rough.

Q55.text: That the time horizon is brutal and nobody tells you upfront. You think you're signing up for 3-4 years and you come out the other side 5-6 years later wondering where your late 20s went. I wish someone had just been straight with me about the real completion timeline before I committed.

Q60.text: The funding model is fundamentally broken and I dont think any amount of reform fixes it without blowing up the incentive structure entirely. But I guess nobody in charge wants to hear that. I just hope whoever reads these responses actually does something with them and doesn't file it away in some department folder never to be opened again. Good luck with the research I guess.

Q17.text: Honestly not much, but if I'm being fair -- the intellectual freedom is real. Nobody tells you what to think about or how to solve the problem, and that's genuinely rare. Some days I'll go down a rabbit hole for hours just because I'm curious and that's technically my job. I don't take that for granted. It's just a shame that everything surrounding it -- the admin, the politics, the funding circus -- makes it so hard to actually enjoy.

Q26.label: Overall, how would you describe the academic system, based on your PhD experience so far?
Q26.text: It is not beneficial for people who want to start working and actually do something. Also not beneficial for entrepreneurial pursuits and multidisciplinary collaboration. It is isolated and particular. Thus, depending on what you study you will either have great skills to market to industry prospects or none at all.

Q16.label: Is there anything else not mentioned that has concerned you since you started your PhD?
Q16.text: What the hell is the point? You do your four years in undergraduate studies and then start graduate studies. Your professors are usually just as mediocre as your undergraduate professors and you have to complete this core curriculum which is just undergraduate extended. So, not only did you have to work your butt off for four years and then complete graduate examinations. But then, you have to repeat the process for about 1.5 years in graduate school. THEN you're completely free to do research. But, you have about 3 years to become sufficiently good enough to contribute. You do this and that only to write a dissertation about an esoteric topic that nobody else will ever care about. Meanwhile, people who didn't do graduate school have been in the workplace this entire time working and gaining experience doing real-world work. You get this degree to work in the world without ever learning how to. Graduate school is mostly a sham.

Q26.text: The academic system, at least how I experience it here in Czech Republic, is deeply oriented toward productivity metrics -- publications, grants, impact factor -- and I think it has lost the connection with the real purpose of science, which is to build knowledge through careful hypothesis and argumentation. There are good researchers who still care about ideas, but the institution rewards quantity above quality. For me, science should begin with a good question, not with a method looking for a problem, and honestly it's kind of exhausting that this perspective is not more valued.

Q41.text: I want to lead my own research group in oncology, working on questions that actually matter rather than just producing output to fill a CV. Q60.text:
I just want to say that I appreciate surveys like this one, because I think the experience of PhD students is often not really listened to by the people who design the academic system. We are treated sometimes more like productive units than as people who are genuinely trying to understand something. I hope the data here can be useful to change something, even if small. Science needs to recover its philosophical backbone, and that starts with asking the right questions -- including about its own institutions.

Pedro

Q17.text: Honestly, what I enjoy most is the freedom to spend time seriously thinking about a problem -- not just executing a protocol, but actually sitting with a question and trying to understand it from different angles. There are moments, not frequent but real, when a reading or a conversation opens something unexpected and you feel that science is doing what it should do. I also appreciate the people, some colleagues here have a genuine intellectual curiosity that is kind of rare to find, and those conversations make the whole experience worth it despite everything else.

Q26.label: Overall, how would you describe the academic system, based on your PhD experience so far?
Q26.text: O sistema acadêmico da república tcheca é bastante focado em produção.  Não se importa muito a defesa de uma tese, da ideia em si.  Apenas vejo que o programas de PhD em geral esqueceram da onde vem a sigla Ph.D e não discutem mais as coisas no âmbito argumentativo.  Não importam tanto com o racional do projeto, com a hipótese do projeto... e a defesa argumentativa que deveria ser feita.  Maioria dos projetos vejo que começa simplesmente por que temos dinheiro e estrutura. Mas não porque temos um grande racional e uma justificativa para tentar lançar uma hipótese a ser defendida por provas a posteriori.    Na minha concepção,  Tudo deveria iniciar com uma ideia sólida.  Uma hipótese a qual todos não consigam derrubar com argumentos. Sendo interessante alocar recursos escassos para responder uma pergunta da qual necessita-se de uma resposta a posteriori.    O sistema então acaba valorizando bastante dados soltos, contudo ainda sim são resultados. E acaba desvalorizando o tempo 'perdido' no campo das ideias.   A quantidade muitas vezes parece ser mais importante do que a qualidade . Infelizmente vejo que o sistema recompensa este tipo de mentalidade.  No Brasil (país onde fiz meu mestrado), não era diferente.   Com isso , o sistema que criamos é um sistema preocupado com técnicos. Pessoas que vangloriam por saber determinada técnica.  Pois em teoria, isto traz mais produção.  As pessoas não entendem que aprender técnica é apenas uma questão de tempo e prática. Não precisa de raciocínio lógico. Sendo que em muitos institutos grandes, você de fato tem técnicos e facilities para fazer o trabalho técnico para você.   No entanto, técnica pode ser aplicada mil vezes... mas se não estiver denfendendo uma ideia não fará nenhum sentido fazer por fazer.   Acredito que precisamos fazer um esforço para mudar esta mentalidade nos institutos ao redor do mundo.  A revista Nature é muito conceituada e acredito que ela representa bem a amostragem dos institutos que de fato estão preocupados em mover o mundo através de ideias.    Pedro Zeni

Q26.text: Deeply flawed -- not incidentally, but by design. The incentives reward output volume and self-promotion over genuine scientific quality, and the people who succeeded in that system often don't recognise that landscape has shifted considerably since their own training. Job prospects are worse, funding is tighter, and the mentorship on offer frequently reflects a different era. It's pretty difficult to feel optimistic about it rn.

Q55.text: How stark the gap is between what a PhD trains you for and what job market actually offers. Q41.text: Science-adjacent roles outside academia -- science communication, policy, or industry research positions where the work is rigorous but the incentive structure isn't quite so punishing. Q60.text: Mostly just that I hope this kind of data actually feeds into something -- the structural problems I've described aren't unique to me, and I think researchers and institutions are often slow to acknowledge how much the experience has deteriorated for current students compared to even a decade ago. The gap between the ideals of scientific inquiry and the day-to-day reality of doing a PhD is pretty significant, and it doesn't get talked about honestly enough. I dont have a tidy solution to offer, but I do think taking these experiences seriously is a necessary starting point.

Q26.text: Intellectually stimulating but structurally broken, honestly. The system is extraordinarily good at training people who want to stay inside it -- but if your ambitions point outward, toward industry or leadership, you're essentially navigating that on your own. Q60.text: I think a lot of the uncertainty about phD careers arises from the vastly different experience each trainee has during graduate school. For example, one trainee may work 70 hours per week, manage a budget, run multiple projects at once, and publish 4 first-author publications as well as a handful of non-first author publications. Meanwhile, another trainee in the same department might work 30 hours per week on their own personal project, is well-read, becomes a member in multiple peer groups/societies, maintains a vibrant social life and extracurricular agenda, and overall is a more well-rounded person. While the first person is likely to move on to a competitive academic post-doc, which of these two is most competitive for the non-academic position? Would one of these trainees out perform the other in a non-academic position? How does the public perceive these two candidates? Do they recognize the merits of each, or would they solely focus on the fact that this person has a phD?
